candidates.name: Estonian Open Air Museum
candidates.price: Winter (September 29 – April 22): Adult €12, Concession €10, Family €25, Evening (1600-) €6, Evening Family (1600-) €12. Summer (April 23 – September 28): Adult €16, Concession €10, Family €28, Evening (1800-) €8, Evening Family (1800-) €16
candidates.content: This museum includes 72 buildings of Estonian vernacular architecture and village milieu of the Tsarist time of rule in a dark, dense forest. This museum provides a picture of the life and its hardship in the old times. The Folklo

candidates.name: Toompea Castle
candidates.content: Seat of Estonian Parliament (Riigikogu). The castle complex consists of several parts: the western wall and the towers of Tall Hermann, Pilsticker and Landskrone built by the Danes between 13th and 15th centuries; the classic styl

candidates.name: Tallinn Linnahall
candidates.content: A fine example of Soviet Brutalist architecture designed by Raine Karp and Riina Altmäe and built for the 22nd Moscow Summer Olympic Games in 1980 for sailing events held in Tallinn. Scale the exterior of this crumbling monumental

candidates.name: Kiek in de Kök
candidates.content: An artillery tower, which is today a museum.

candidates.name: St. Olaf's church
candidates.content: Built in the 12th century. Today it is a Baptist church and probably the most visible landmark on the northern end of the Old Town. When Estonia was part of the Soviet Union the tower was used as a radio tower and a surveillance p

candidates.name: St. Nicholas church
candidates.content: St.Olaf's lookalike is at the other end of the Old Town. Heavily damaged in World War II and a fire in the 1980s, it is now an art museum and houses Bernt Notke's famous Danse Macabre from 1633.

candidates.name: Vabamu
candidates.content: Educates and involves the people of Estonia and its visitors and encourages everyone to think about the recent past, to sense the fragility of freedom, and to stand for freedom and justice.

candidates.name: City Wall
candidates.content: A section of the City Wall can be climbed from the corner of Suur-Kloostri and Väike-Kloostri, with entry into three towers possible. Quite frankly, the views from up on Toompea are better, and the spiral staircases are steep and

candidates.name: Estonian History Museum
candidates.content: The History Museum's main location is the medieval Great Guild Hall. Here, the permanent exhibition takes you through 11,000 years of Estonian history by means ranging from striking exhibits of artifacts to interactive "time capsu

candidates.name: Estonian Maritime Museum
candidates.content: The Maritime Museum dates back to 1935 and is housed inside the largest of the Tallinn city wall towers, aptly named "Fat Margaret" (Paks Margareta). Visiting the museum allows one not only to see the potpourri of maritime-themed

candidates.name: KGB Prison cells museum
candidates.content: Now the Interior Ministry and not generally open to the public, this is where the KGB detained and tortured suspected dissidents. A Soviet-era joke says that this was the tallest building in Estonia: even from the basement, you co

candidates.name: Contemporary Art Museum of Estonia (EKKM)
candidates.hours: April to December: Tue–Sun 12:00–19:00 (you may want to double-check online)
candidates.content: Already when entering, this place plays with what a museum should look like: you enter into a café. The exhibition rooms are diverse, as they make use of old industrial space. The shows are prepared by artists, hence the place bui

candidates.name: Kadriorg Palace
candidates.content: An imperial Russian summer residence built by Italian architect Niccolo Michetti for Tsar Peter the Great in 1718. It is in a 90-ha (222-acre) park in the eastern part of the city. The Tsar, a classic and mysterious Russian soul,

candidates.name: National Art Museum KUMU
candidates.content: Opened in 2006, this is the largest government-built building since the liberation and it is an almost 50,000 m² (538,196 ft²). The museum, whose architecture is by itself enough to justify the visit, houses a cyclopic house, part

candidates.name: Seaplane Harbour
candidates.hours: May-Sep: daily 10:00 to 19:00; Oct – Apr: Tue-Sun 10:00 to 18:00
candidates.content: Lennusadam, literally "air port", was constructed in 1916 for the purpose of serving the seaplane fleet with a spectacular, three-domed concrete hangar. Today, it serves as an outpost of the Maritime museum, serving its large coll

candidates.name: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral
candidates.content: A classic onion-domed Russian Orthodox church, built 1894–1900, during the Russification period when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire. In 1928, when Estonia was independent, it was argued that the church is a symbol of oppre

candidates.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
candidates.content: The oldest church in Tallinn, built as a Catholic church in 1229, but renovated and expanded many times since then. It became a Lutheran church in 1561.

candidates.name: Viru Gate
candidates.content: This section of town is known as All-Linn or "Lower Town", as it's where the merchants and artisans of old Tallinn lived. Today, Viru is still Tallinn's trendiest shopping street and the entire All-Linn is the busiest (and most to

candidates.name: Town Hall Square
candidates.content: The square in the heart of the Old Town, just next to medieval Town Hall (Raekoda), ringed with cafes and restaurants. The square was used as a marketplace.

candidates.name: Town Hall
candidates.content: Tallinn Town Hall, built at the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries, is the oldest town hall in the Nordic countries and Baltic states. Its heavy stone structure dominates the square. Nowadays it's used as a museum where smaller c

candidates.name: City Train for kids
candidates.content: Departs every 20 minutes; so takes the round trip.

candidates.name: Freedom Square
candidates.content: The Freedom Square is one of the main squares in Tallinn, featuring the simple and elegant St. John's Church from the 1860s and the contemporary Victory Column, erected in 2009 to commemorate the Estonian War of Independence of 19

candidates.name: Rottermann Quarter
candidates.content: An industrial district between the city and the Tallinn Port. The buildings are from the 19th and 20th century, with motifs of Art Nouveau and Historicism. New and stylish apartment buildings with shopping centre have now been bui

candidates.name: Peter the Great's Naval Fortress
candidates.content: In the 18th century, the coastal protection batteries, part of the larger Peter the Great’s sea fortress system, were built in the island.

candidates.name: Tallinn TV Tower
candidates.content: A 314 m high, free-standing structure with an observation deck on the 21st floor which, with its 170 m, is the highest in Northern Europe. It offers spectacular views across Tallinn and, on a clear day, you can see Finland.

candidates.name: Tallinn Botanical Gardens
candidates.hours: Visitor center 10-19, outdoor gardens 09-20, greenhouses 11-19, territory closes every day at 21
candidates.content: The Tallinn Botanic Garden is in the eastern outskirts of Tallinn, 10 km from the city centre and 3 km from the Pirita Sailing and Recreation Centre.It is a must see destination for nature and plant lovers. The "greenhou

candidates.name: Tallinn Zoo
candidates.content: This is an enormous area. Among its live exhibits, you'll find the world's best collections of mountain goats and sheep, which means there are a lot of them! Tallinn Zoo defies the realities of a relatively modest town -- it featu

candidates.name: Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF)
candidates.content: The festival combines a feature film festival with the sub-festivals of animated films, student films and children/youth films.

candidates.name: Medieval Days
candidates.content: Come and experience the medieval atmosphere of the historic Hanseatic City! You can find workshops and market with traders, participate in tours and witness exciting tournaments.

candidates.name: Pikakari Beach
candidates.content: The water quality is fairly good and it gets deep quite soon when you go in. The huge waves coming from the ships break on shore for the joy of all swimmers. The historical Katariina Pier is nice to walk on.

candidates.name: The Estonian Song Celebration
candidates.content: First held in 1869, takes place every five years. In 2014, 35,000 choral singers gathered to perform for an audience of 90,000 people. It is recognised by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Ti

candidates.name: Tallinn Music Week
candidates.content: Showcase festival, aiming to stage the best and most outstanding Estonian talent on two nights in Tallinn's most vibrant live venues, as well as a networking event for the music industry professionals.

candidates.name: Saku Suurhall
candidates.content: Rocca al Mare. Estonia's largest concert and exhibition space, the venue for the 2002 Eurovision Song Contest. The hall and its facilities include an excellent shopping centre that can easily be reached by trolleybus 6.

candidates.name: Kalev Spa
candidates.content: One of the largest water parks in Northern Estonia.

candidates.name: Pirita Beach
candidates.content: A large sandy beach which in summer is full of locals and tourists.

candidates.name: Simpel Session
candidates.content: International skateboarding and BMX event.

candidates.name: Tallinn International Festival Jazzkaar
candidates.content: In addition to Tallinn, jazz concerts also take place in Tartu and Pärnu.

candidates.name: Birgitta Festival
candidates.content: Music and theatre festival, held at the ruins of the historical Pirita (St. Bridget's) convent.

candidates.name: Atlantis H2O Aquapark
candidates.content: The water park has several fun water equipment: a wave pool, a flow pool and eight different slides, the longest of which is over 120 m. For toddlers, there is a separate area with two smaller slides, a climbing area and a 0.20-m-

candidates.name: Vembu-Tembumaa
candidates.content: The oldest and largest amusement park for the whole family.

candidates.name: Lake Harku
candidates.content: Small lake that draws a lot of people. The lake gets dirtier by the year and swimming is not always recommended. Watch out for the vipers on the shore!

candidates.name: Kultuurikatel (creative hub)
candidates.content: A former industrial site, it now Tallinn's main creative hub, site of many events (see website).

candidates.name: PROTO Invention Factory
candidates.content: Indoor amusement park where amusements take place with the help of VR glasses.

candidates.name: Stroomi Beach
candidates.content: The water is clean and warm, and it is the gay friendliest beach of Tallinn.

candidates.name: Kakumäe beach
candidates.content: The water is one of the purest in all of Tallinn beaches.

candidates.name: Riff
candidates.content: If Russian club music, vodka shots and a vibrant crowd is your desire, this is the base. Pretty empty until 01:00 after then it fills up. They have a nice terrace during summer which is a popular meeting point as the main bus term

candidates.name: Teater
candidates.content: Basement club on Vabaduse square. Popular with late twens and smaller groups. Music focus is on 1990s and 2000s. Door policy is relaxed but most people are dressed up. Usually starts going at midnight.

candidates.name: Beer House
candidates.content: Plenty of beers to choose from in this large authentically styled and decorated Bavarian Beer hall, including 5 of their own beers made on site. Try the Medovar Honey beer.

candidates.name: Drink Baar
candidates.content: The widest selection of beers of any pub in town including many quality imports from Brewdog and Mikkeller. Good English-style pub-grub, featuring award winning fish and chips. Monthly comedy nights from the "Comedy Estonia" and q

candidates.name: Hell Hunt
candidates.content: The name means "the gentle wolf" in Estonian. A comfortable and homey pub in the Old Town and offers a wide selection of beers (including two of their own brews) and some pretty decent food. Don't miss the spare ribs.

candidates.name: Helsinki Karaoke Baar
candidates.content: A legendary gathering place for Finns. This bar, also known as Lokaal Helsinki, is a popular destination for both locals and tourists who crave a cozy atmosphere and Finnish music.

candidates.name: 100 õlle koht
candidates.content: The name means "the place of 100 beers" and the establishment indeed serves over 100 different types of beer. Traditional Estonian pub snacks also available. It's in an underground cellar so it's not suitable for people with limit

candidates.name: Texas Honky Tonk & Cantina
candidates.content: Texas-style cantina is a casual place for a Corona or, if you must, a Bud, or even to try out the frozen margaritas churning in the electric mixer behind the bar. More serious drinkers can try the "tequila flights": 3 or 5 shots o

candidates.name: Piana Vyshnia
candidates.content: A bar that serves only one kind of drink, so it's easy to decide what to get: a moderately sweet, cognac-infused spirit on cherries (the name means "The Drunk Cherry"). You won't find anything like it anywhere else.

candidates.name: Lounge 24
candidates.content: On the top floor of the Radisson Blu Hotel, it offers spectacular views of Old Town and the Baltic sea from a trendy indoor setting and a breathtaking outdoor terrace. Lounge 24 serves a variety of light fares to full dinner menu,

candidates.name: Hollywood
candidates.content: Big club, popular with young Estonians during the week (Ladies Night on Wednesday) and general party crowd at the weekend. Standard is euro trash and top40 songs. Gets started at 23:00 but before 01:00 the party doesn't rock.

candidates.name: Prive
candidates.content: Tallinn's flashiest nightspot, run by legendary warehouse party organizers Vibe, often has foreign DJs playing. Expensive and has strict face control, so dress up.

candidates.name: Virgins
candidates.content: Gentlemen's club with erotic shows and luxurious drinks. Popular with business travellers and male tourists.

candidates.name: The Dubliner
candidates.content: Popular Irish pub on one of the nightlife axes. Attracts younger people and is relatively new, so no pub crawlers puke in front of the door.

candidates.sec: East of the old town around the Coca-Cola Plaza
candidates.name: Kohvik Narva
candidates.price: Cake per kg €8.50-12, pastry pieces €0.70, solyanka €3, pancake €2.50-3.50, pasta carbonara €6, schnitzel €7, potato fritter €3-5, Pelmeni €5
candidates.content: Cafe Narva long boasted an old-style interior preserved from the Soviet area; today's chic interior seems questionably authentic. Ladies at the counter are somewhat brusque (still) and mostly Russian-speaking, although this should

candidates.name: Cinnamon
candidates.content: An Indian and European mix cuisine in the Tallinn Old Town. Serves international cuisine for tourists' tastes, don't expect traditional Estonian cuisine here. You can eat either inside or at the (rather cramped) terrace on Pikk st

candidates.name: Kaja Pizza Köök
candidates.price: pizza 5-8 Euro + 1 Euro per additional topping
candidates.hours: Tue - Sun 11:30 till Out of Dough (they will make a given amount of dough every day, so if it's very busy they will close "early")
candidates.content: pizza baked in a wood oven, with the choice of topping being aligned to traditional south Italian pizza. Small place, just one big table everybody shares. Combining traditional elements and a rather modern/hip atmosphere.

candidates.name: Kohvik Moon
candidates.content: A rather small restaurant with a nice, minimalistic decor. Serves traditional Estonian food with a Russian influence. Voted best restaurant in Tallinn in 2010. Very popular among tourists, and as such it is usually quite full. Pri

candidates.name: Kompressor
candidates.content: This place offers an assortment of huge and delicious pancakes. Don't give in to the temptation to order two portions, one pancake is usually enough. This place used to be less touristic, but is now.

candidates.name: Kuldse Notsu Kõrts
candidates.content: Good traditional Estonian restaurant close to the main square. Try the house beer or vodka and fresh buckthorn and honey apertif with your blood sausage or the famous pork knuckle with extra spicy mustard. The traditional desserts

candidates.name: Tchaikovsky
candidates.content: As the name suggests, it is a Russian restaurant, but don't expect wooden benches, traditional food, and folk music. On the contrary, you will find a selection of Russian delicacies ranging from pancakes with caviar to pelmeni wit

candidates.name: Maiasmokk
candidates.content: The oldest still operating café in Tallinn, dating back to 1864. Coffee, tea, chocolate and various sweet and savoury pastries at quite cheap prices. Spacious with stylish decor. Next door is the Maiasmokk confectionery shop, whic

candidates.sec: Around the market Balti Jaama Turg
candidates.name: F-hoone
candidates.hours: Mon-Sat 9-24, Sun 9-22; kitchen closes 1 hr earlier
candidates.content: Used to be an industrial hall, now made a great bistro/bar which tends to become very busy in the evenings (book if you can, but as it's big you might well be lucky and find the one spare table. Good value for price.

candidates.name: Oliver
candidates.content: A traditional restaurant in the heart of the Tallinn Old town. The menu is centered on various kinds of steaks, but there are also pastas and vegetarian dishes available. Main courses €15–23.

candidates.name: Restoran Peppersack
candidates.content: A middle ages-themed restaurant one block away from Raekoja plats – even the names of the dishes are medieval themed. Outdoor seating available in the summer, when they also played medieval (what else?) music on a small outdoor st

candidates.name: Pirosmani
candidates.content: Georgian food as it is done in Georgia. It's well out of the way, but that's a good thing. Almost everyone at this restaurant is local (although the menu has English), and tourists are not in sight, so the food here is good and gr

candidates.name: Rocca al Mare kaubanduskeskus
candidates.content: A few kilometres west of the old town along Paldiski maantee. Consists of a Prisma hypermarket and tens of smaller, mostly fashion boutiques. Also restaurants.

candidates.name: Jaama Turg
candidates.content: A market place next to the train station. Overrated and overpriced, gourmet food at three times the price of regular market places. For tourist and rich locals.

candidates.name: Jõuluturg
candidates.content: The Christmas Market on the Town Hall square is open from late November to early January. They sell knitwear, various wooden objects for use and decoration, Christmas tree decorations, gingerbread and such. It's not all about shop

candidates.name: Vana Turg
candidates.content: The name translates to "old market" and is located on a small square just outside the old town. Vana Turg is a place to buy clothes and decoration items often Estonian-made and sometimes sold by the makers themselves: knitted pull

candidates.name: Sadamarket
candidates.content: Shopping daytrippers who arrive with Viking Line or Eckerö Line and can't be bothered to walk far from the terminal usually end up at this large indoor market. Three floors of clothing, bags, food and souvenirs plus some restauran

december.text: At these latitudes winters are dark and cold and temperatures under −20°C (−5°F) are not unheard of from December to February. Thankfully, the sea moderates the winter temperatures a bit.

Usually you will need your jacket again towards the latter half of September. The autumn is the "rainy season" and with both temperatures and the leaves falling, Tallinn doesn't look very attractive this time of the year. However the greyness is covered up by the snow that usually arrives in early December. Visiting Ta
